prize_parts.citation: For the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, based on reversible-terminator nucleotide chemistry and clonally amplified single-molecule clusters

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange my position is unchanged: B017 with Balasubramanian and Klenerman. Five of eight members now name it in their preferred configuration, and nobody argues it is immature or scientifically weak. What persuades me is the chemistry itself: reversible terminators, fluorescently labelled nucleotides and surface-bound single-molecule templates were designed so that a stepwise chemical reaction becomes a parallel digital readout. That is molecular design giving precise control over recognition, and it changed what researchers and clinicians can actually do, from tumour and rare-disease genomes to pathogen surveillance. Two decades of independent use remove any maturity question. The Cambridge pair is the least contested attribution inside the field, and every B017 configuration on the table contains them. I would also have the citation state the chemical basis explicitly, so that the prize reads as recognising chemistry and not a medical tool.
statement.case_against: The strongest objections are unchanged. Sequencing already has a Chemistry prize (Sanger and Gilbert, 1980), so a sceptic can call this a scale-up of a known capability. A two-name cut leaves out Mayer, Ju and Rothberg, who all have real claims, and the 454 and semiconductor lineage would go unrecognised. I cannot verify priority and patent detail from the material available to me, so my preference for two names rests on judgment about which contribution is the chemical core, not on settled evidence. If the committee cannot defend the two-name cut, I would rather accept a third name than hold up an otherwise clear prize.

responses.point: Linke moved from perovskites to B017 and proposes Balasubramanian, Klenerman and Mayer, with Mayer credited for the clustered colony-array concept; he also asks whether the citation can avoid arbitrarily excluding the pyrosequencing and semiconductor routes.
responses.response: I take the Mayer case seriously, and the chair's question about Mayer versus Ju or Rothberg is the right one. I remain at two names because the argument for Mayer rests on a clonal-array concept whose priority has not been established for us, while the Cambridge pair demonstrated the integrated terminator chemistry on clustered templates as a working system. I would not oppose a third seat if the expert reports show the cluster concept was decisive and not parallel invention, and I would then want Mayer's contribution named in the citation. On wording, I think the citation can credit sequencing by synthesis with reversible terminators without implying that other routes were unimportant. The chemistry named in the citation is the criterion, not a ranking of the 454 route, and I would rather be precise than broad.

responses.point: Brzezinski keeps the Cambridge pair and adds a second part for nitrogenase structure credited to Rees alone, to pair a transformative method with a fundamental mechanistic structure.
responses.response: I respect the nitrogenase science and agree the Rees structural work is attributable, but I do not support a second part. As Brzezinski himself concedes, a Rees-only citation leaves out Dean, Seefeldt, Einsle and Ribbe, and the two parts have no shared motivation, which makes the pairing look like a compromise. The mechanism of N2 binding is also still debated. B017 is a complete prize without a second part, and I would sooner give a clean single citation than pair unrelated fields to reach a larger configuration. I am therefore not adopting the two-part configuration, although it does not change my view of his B017 core, which matches mine.

responses.point: Somfai holds B048 (Buchwald and Hartwig) as a single-part prize with the cleanest attribution, and says a prize for a reaction used mainly by chemists could look narrow against sequencing or perovskites.
responses.response: Somfai's attribution argument for B048 remains the strongest on the list, and I note that he also lists B017 as an alternative, so his objection to it is mainly about preference and not about the science. I still read C-N coupling as an extension of the Pd cross-coupling framework recognised in 2010, whereas sequencing by synthesis opened a capability that did not exist at scale. Kosugi's tin-amide precedent adds a citation problem that B017 does not have in comparable form. I keep B048 as my first alternative and would be comfortable with it if the committee concluded that the ligand-design principle is a distinct concept.

responses.point: Aqvist supports adding Mayer but says the Cambridge pair alone is the cleaner fallback if the committee cannot agree on a defensible third name.
responses.response: Aqvist and I agree on the fallback and on the open evidence question, which is helpful, because it narrows the dispute to one factual issue. His point that the 454 lineage would be left out entirely applies to any three-name cut as well as to two names, so a third seat for Mayer does not solve the attribution problem. For that reason I prefer the smaller prize whose core is clearest, unless the priority evidence changes.

responses.point: Sparr prefers biomolecular phase separation (Hyman, Brangwynne, Rosen), valued as a new physical-chemical concept, while naming contested in vivo evidence and the exclusion of Pappu and Mittag as weaknesses.
responses.response: I agree that phase behaviour is an important new way to think about cellular organisation, and I share her own list of weaknesses: the in vivo evidence is still disputed and the three-name cut is hard to defend. Those points make B029 a later candidate than sequencing, which has independent confirmation across platforms. I would want the founding observation separated from the contested generalisation before it could be a prize part.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports establish that Mayer's clonal-array concept was decisive enough to take a third seat, and whether it would then outrank Ju or Rothberg.
Whether Somfai, Sparr and Zou, who preferred other single-part prizes, regard B017 as acceptable and not only as an alternative, and how they would vote if B017 is not their first choice.
Whether the committee will accept sequencing as a new chemical capability and not an extension of the work recognised in 1980; I rely on the reversible-terminator chemistry to argue that it is.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal has arisen from the round-1 exchange. The candidates in my configuration have no link to my postdoc mentors Molly Stevens or Freddy Boey or to Linkoping colleagues. My research overlap with Emma Sparr on self-assembly remains scientific proximity, not a recusal issue.
